main_damage_causes: Complete erasure of Phineas Nigellus's personality and voice: his sole film appearance gives him no dialogue and no characterisation, reducing a distinctively drawn character to a silent prop

Absence of the extended tent/Deathly Hallows-era scenes from the book corpus, which represent the fullest realisation of his character, his blood prejudice, his pride, and his plot-functional role regarding the sword of Gryffindor
No establishment of his antagonistic dynamic with Harry or his emotional investment in the Black family legacy, leaving the character without any relational texture

damaging_scenes.scene: Film – Dumbledore's office scene: Dumbledore instructs 'Phineas' to go to Grimmauld Place
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the books, Phineas Nigellus is a distinct, sharply characterised presence in Dumbledore's office portraits – supercilious, sardonic, hissing at impertinence, vocally opinionated about students and blood status. He is referred to by his full name 'Phineas Nigellus' and his personality is a notable texture in any scene he appears in.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film reduces Phineas Nigellus to a single functional line where Dumbledore addresses him only as 'Phineas' and instructs him to carry a message to Grimmauld Place. He receives no dialogue, no reaction, no characterisation whatsoever – he is used purely as a plot relay device with no personality on display.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book establishes Phineas Nigellus as one of the most distinctive portrait personalities – arrogant, classist, and entertainingly contrary. Reducing his sole film appearance to a mute errand boy strips away all of that voice and personality, making him an unnamed prop rather than a character.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film – Dumbledore's office scene: Phineas given no reaction, no dialogue, no characterisation
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book corpus shows Phineas Nigellus consistently interjecting with unsolicited commentary ('Impertinent,' hissing at Harry's questions, calling Hermione 'simple girl,' expressing outrage at Mundungus stealing Black heirlooms, walking out of his frame in indignation). He has agency and a distinct voice even in brief appearances.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Phineas is addressed and presumably complies, but is given no lines, no reaction shot, and no opportunity to express any of his established personality. His compliance is treated as automatic and silent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: A character who in the books never misses an opportunity to voice his opinions and assert his superiority is rendered entirely passive and voiceless. This removes his function as a source of dry, aristocratic commentary and his role as a minor but memorable antagonistic presence in the headmaster's office.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film – entire film: absence of Phineas Nigellus's extended tent/camping scene interactions
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book corpus contains an extended scene (Scenes 12–44) in which Phineas Nigellus is blindfolded, interrogated by Harry and Hermione, argues back, insults Hermione as 'simple girl' and 'Muggle-born,' is called supercilious by the narration, reveals key intelligence about the sword of Gryffindor (goblin-silver absorbing only that which strengthens it), and ultimately refuses to return – all while in a portrait being carried by the trio. This scene establishes his relationship with Harry, his pride, his blood prejudice, and delivers plot-critical information.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This entire interaction is absent from the film corpus. None of the tent scenes, the blindfolded portrait, the sword-of-Gryffindor intelligence, or any of the characterisation from these extended exchanges appears.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is the single scene in the corpus where Phineas Nigellus is most fully realised as a character – showing his blood prejudice, his pride, his reluctant utility to Harry, and his complicated loyalty to the Black family legacy. Its absence means the audience never sees him as anything other than a messenger, losing both his characterisation and his contribution to the Horcrux/sword plot thread.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film – entire film: absence of Phineas Nigellus's role in the Mundungus/Black heirlooms subplot
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 7 shows Phineas Nigellus erupting in genuine outrage – 'That mangy old half-blood has been stealing Black heirlooms?' – and storming out of his frame to go to Grimmauld Place. This reveals both his fierce pride in the Black family legacy and a dimension of his character beyond mere compliance with Dumbledore.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: No such scene or reaction appears in the film corpus. Phineas's emotional investment in the Black family honour is entirely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The moment of Phineas storming out in indignation over stolen Black heirlooms is one of his most vivid characterisation beats – it shows he has genuine feeling and personal stakes beyond his role as Dumbledore's messenger. Its absence flattens him to a purely functional instrument.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film – Dumbledore's office: Phineas's relationship with Harry and Hogwarts student body never established
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 2 and 4 show Phineas Nigellus reacting to Harry's questions with hissing disapproval and the word 'Impertinent,' establishing a clear antagonistic attitude toward students and a contempt for Harry specifically that is part of his recurring dynamic throughout the series.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film gives Phineas no interaction with Harry at all; Dumbledore speaks to him and he is presumably off-screen complying. No antagonism, no condescension, no dynamic with Harry is established.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The low-level antagonism between Phineas and Harry – Phineas disapproving of Harry's impertinence, Harry managing him with flattery – is a running texture in the books. The film establishes none of this, so any future interactions (in later films) would lack grounding.
